interps.citation: Paskon v. Wright, 230 S.W.3d 24 (Mo. App. E.D. 2007)
interps.summary: Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District opinion applying or construing Rule 74.05, Rule 81.07, Rule 78.06 (neutral index summary; see verbatim excerpts).
excerpts: Pursuant to Rule 74.05(d), this Court treats a motion to set aside a judgment in two distinct manners depending upon when the motion was filed. As in this case, when a motion to set aside is filed within thirty days of the entry of the default judgment, it is treated as an authorized after-trial motion and “is deemed the equivalent of a motion for new trial.” Id. Therefore, the motion to set aside extends the trial court’s jurisdiction over the default judgment for ninety days from the date the motion was filed. Miller v. Rothschild Management Group, 184 S.W.3d 575, 577 (Mo.App. E.D.2005).
Subsequently, Wright filed a motion to appeal out of time with this Court on October 4, 2006, pursuant to Rule 81.07(a).

Hence, if this motion had been filed after January 1, 2007, the motion would not have been deemed denied pursuant to Rule 78.06 and the trial court could have taken up the motion on the merits four months after it was filed. . Rule 81.07(a) states: When an appeal is permitted by law from a judgment in the trial court, but the time prescribed for filing an ordinary notice of appeal with the clerk of the trial court as set forth in Rule 81.04 has expired, a party may seek a special order of the appropriate appellate court permitting a late filing of the notice of appeal. The special order may be allowed by the appellate court only upon motion with notice to the adverse parties filed within six months from the date the judgment appealed from became final for purposes of appeal and only upon a showing by affidavit, or otherwise, that the delay was not due to appellant's culpable negligence.

norms.b_justification: The opinion (2007-07-24) predates the current version of Rule 74.05 (in force since 2016-01-01) but quotes the language it applies — “not intentionally or recklessly designed to impede the judicial process.” — and that language appears verbatim (normalized for punctuation/case) in the current text; the interpreted language is therefore identical in wording and function.

interps.court: Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District
interps.citation: Chad v. City of Lake Ozark, 223 S.W.3d 208 (Mo. App. W.D. 2007)
interps.summary: Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District opinion applying or construing Rule 84.14 (neutral index summary; see verbatim excerpts).
excerpts: In other words, depending on the interpretation given to § 105.370 and § 79.240, either the motion for summary judgment for the respondent or the appellant should have been granted. And, because we interpret the ordinance and the statute in the appellant’s favor, pursuant to Rule 84.14, we reverse and direct the trial court to enter summary judgment for the appellant on his writ.

The argument would be that, in declaring that summary judgment should have been granted to the party whose motion was denied by the trial court, the appellate court is doing so as part and parcel of its authorized review and ruling on the trial court’s grant of summary judgment to the adverse party and in accordance with Rule 84.14, which authorizes the appellate court to declare the judgment that the trial court ought to have given.

interps.court: Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District
interps.citation: In the Interest of K.T.K. v. Crawford County Juvenile Office, 229 S.W.3d 196 (Mo. App. S.D. 2007)
interps.summary: Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District opinion applying or construing § 211.455, § 211.447 RSMo (neutral index summary; see excerpts).
excerpts: A.P.K. (“Father”), natural father of K.T.K., K.A.K., A.K., and I.K. (collectively referred to as the “children”), appeals the termination of his parental rights, contending the juvenile court erred when it found that there were statutory grounds to do so, and in not strictly complying with the provisions of Section 211.455.

On June 7, 2006, the juvenile court entered its “Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law and Judgment,” terminating the parental rights of Mother and Father, finding that statutory grounds existed for termination under Sections 211.447.4(2) and 211.447.4(3), and that termination was in the children’s best interest.

In his second point, Father argues that the juvenile court erred in terminating his parental rights, because it did not comply with the requirement of Section 211.455.1 that, “[w]ithin thirty days after the filing of the petition, the juvenile officer shall meet with the court in order to determine that all parties have been served with summons and to request that the court order the investigation and social study.”
Section 211.447 authorizes the termination of parental rights if the trial court finds at least one statutory ground for termination exists and that termination is in the best interest of the child.

norms.b_justification: The opinion (2007-05-23) applied § 211.455 RSMo as in force from 1985-09-28 (revisor bid 58713) and cites subsection(s) 1; the revisor version comparison (data/mo-history) shows these subsections unchanged in the current text in force since 2014-08-28, so the interpreted language is identical in wording and function.

Functional review: the opinion (2007-05-23) applied § 211.447 RSMo as in force from 1998-07-01 (revisor bid 58712); current text in force since 2021-08-28. Interpreted subsection(s) identified from the opinion: 4, 4. Compared subsection 4: version text “4. The juvenile officer or the division may file a petition to terminate the parental rights of the child's parent when it appears that one or more of the following grounds for termination exist: (1) The child has been a…” / current text “4. If grounds exist for termination of parental rights pursuant to subsection 2 of this section, the juvenile officer or the division may, but is not required to, file a petition to terminate the parental rights of the c…”; subsection 4: version text “4. The juvenile officer or the division may file a petition to terminate the parental rights of the child's parent when it appears that one or more of the following grounds for termination exist: (1) The child has been a…” / current text “4. If grounds exist for termination of parental rights pursuant to subsection 2 of this section, the juvenile officer or the division may, but is not required to, file a petition to terminate the parental rights of the c…”. The opinion interprets the neglect and failure-to-rectify grounds in former subsections 4(2) and 4(3). Those provisions were renumbered to current subsections 5(2) and 5(3) and retain the same operative language and function; the added disability-discrimination sentence does not alter those grounds.

Section 452.375 permits either sole or joint custody; a parent may no longer be granted ‘primary’ legal or physical custody.”

Notably, Rule 94.06 provides: "Any of the parties below may, within the time fixed for the respondent to answer, file an answer to the petition in mandamus or may answer jointly with the respondent or with each other.”

norms.b_justification: Functional review: the opinion (2007-05-23) applied § 452.375 RSMo as in force from 2005-08-28 (revisor bid 51905); current text in force since 2024-08-28. Interpreted subsection(s) identified from the opinion: 5. Compared subsection 5: version text “5. Prior to awarding the appropriate custody arrangement in the best interest of the child, the court shall consider each of the following as follows: (1) Joint physical and joint legal custody to both parents, which sha…” / current text “5. Prior to awarding the appropriate custody arrangement in the best interest of the child, the court shall consider each of the following as follows: (1) Joint physical and joint legal custody to both parents, which sha…”. The opinion interprets subsection 5's authorized custody arrangements, particularly subdivisions (1)–(4), which provide for joint or sole legal and physical custody rather than a separate “primary” custody designation. Those provisions remain substantively identical in the current text; the amendment to subdivision (5) concerns third-party custody and does not alter the interpreted rule.

interps.court: Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District
interps.citation: Pruitt v. Missouri Department of Corrections, 224 S.W.3d 630 (Mo. App. W.D. 2007)
interps.summary: Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District opinion applying or construing § 516.145 RSMo, Rule 67.03 (neutral index summary; see verbatim excerpts).
excerpts: The appeal is dismissed. All concur. . All statutory references are to RSMo. (2000) unless otherwise specified. Section 516.145 provides that “all actions brought by an offender, as defined in section 217.010, RSMo, against the department of corrections or any entity or division thereof, or any employee or former employee for an act in an official capacity, or by the omission of an official duty” must be brought within one year of the event.
Under Rule 67.03, “[a]ny involuntary dismissal shall be without prejudice unless the court in its order for dismissal shall otherwise specify.”
Pruitt does not dispute that he is subject to the limitations set forth in Section 516.145 but rather bases his argument on the date his injury accrued.

The appellate court found these provisions inadequate under sections 452.375.9 and 452.310.7 and remanded the case to provide a more detailed parenting plan.
These provisions are not sufficient for a complete parenting plan under sections 452.375.9 and 452.310.7.

interps.court: Missouri Court of Appeals
interps.citation: Bottorff v. Bottorff, 221 S.W.3d 482 (Mo. App. 2007)

interps.citation: Bottorff v. Bottorff, 221 S.W.3d 482 (Mo. App. S.D. 2007)
interps.summary: Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District opinion applying or construing § 452.375, 78.07, 41.06, 88.01 RSMo (neutral index summary; see excerpts).
excerpts: In essence, father claims that the trial court erred by insufficiently describing in the judgment the basis leading it to conclude that the particular custodial arrangement set forth in the judgment was in the best interest of the children, as required by § 452.375.6.

Rule 78.07(c) provides that “[i]n all cases, allegations of error relating to the form or language of the judgment, including the failure to make statutorily required findings, must be raised in a motion to amend the judgment in order to be preserved for appellate review.”

Under these circumstances, the court concluded that the application of Rule 78.07(c) would work an injustice and, therefore, pursuant to Rule 41.06, the amended Rule 78.07(c) should not be applied to bar appellate review of the failure to make the statutorily required findings.
(citation removed). b) Discussion “When a court determines child support in any proceeding, Rule 88.01 and § 452.340 require it to follow a two step procedure.”

The opinion (2007-05-10) predates the current version of 78.07 (in force since 2017-07-01) but quotes the statutory/rule language it interprets — “including the failure to make statutorily required findings,” — and that language appears verbatim in the current text; the interpreted language is therefore identical in wording and function.

interps.court: Missouri Court of Appeals
interps.citation: Billings Mutual Insurance Co. v. Cameron Mutual Insurance Co., 229 S.W.3d 138 (Mo. App. 2007)
interps.summary: Missouri Court of Appeals opinion applying or construing Rule 55.01 (neutral index summary; see verbatim excerpts).
excerpts: Rule 55.01 also requires that a “defense consisting of an affirmative avoidance to any matter alleged in a preceding pleading must be pleaded.” Thus, once Cameron pleaded the late-notice affirmative defense in its answer, Billings was required to file a reply to that answer if it intended to seek an affirmative avoidance to Cameron’s affirmative defense.

Rule 55.01; Angoff, 917 S.W.2d at 211. b) Alleged Ambiguity in Notice Provisions Billings next claims that the notice provisions of the Policy in section E(2) and the “no-action clause” in section E(4) are ambiguous, and as such, should be construed against Cameron.

As to the latter exception, Cameron timely objected, asserting Billings’ failure to file a reply raising these avoidances, both when Billings asserted the avoidances in arguing the motions for summary judgment, and when Billings attempted to offer evidence on the avoidances at trial. Such timely objections support that Cameron did not consent to the trial of these avoid-ances and did not waive Billings’ obligation to file a reply asserting the avoidances, as required by Rule 55.01.

norms.b_justification: The opinion (2007-05-09) predates the current version of Rule 55.01 (in force since 2010-07-01) but quotes the language it applies — “defense consisting of an affirmative avoidance to any matter alleged in a preceding pleading must be pleaded.” — and that language appears verbatim (normalized for punctuation/case) in the current text; the interpreted language is therefore identical in wording and function.

interps.court: Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District
interps.citation: Masonic Temple Ass'n v. Compass Square & Star, Inc., 229 S.W.3d 134 (Mo. App. E.D. 2007)
interps.summary: Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District opinion applying or construing Rule 74.01 (neutral index summary; see verbatim excerpts).
excerpts: The purpose of Rule 74.01 is “to avoid redundant review of multiple appeals based on the same underlying facts and similar legal issues.”

To allow this appeal would be to directly defeat the purpose of Rule 74.01 because this Court would likely be asked by Appellant to review later judgments awarding attorney’s fees to the other board members.

Where, however, a case involves multiple claims and multiple parties, Rule 74.01 provides an exception to the general rule by allowing a trial court to designate as final a judgment “as to one or more claims but fewer than all claims.”

interps.court: Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District
interps.citation: State ex rel. Nixon v. Bowers, 221 S.W.3d 463 (Mo. App. W.D. 2007)
interps.summary: Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District opinion applying or construing Rule 74.03 (neutral index summary; see verbatim excerpts).
excerpts: If such notice is not given, the order or judgment shall be set aside for good cause shown upon written motion filed within six months from the entry of the order or judgment.... “The purpose of Rule 74.03 is to afford parties time in which to challenge judgments or orders of which they were otherwise unaware.”

He averred that the clerk had failed to mail him notice of the judgment as required by Rule 74.03 and that he was thereby prejudiced because the time for filing an appeal had lapsed. Five days after Bowers filed his motion to set aside the judgment, the circuit court issued an order “reentering” its May 15, 2006 judgment.

In his first point, Bowers claims the circuit court erred in denying his motion to set aside the judgment under Rule 74.03 because the clerk of the court failed to provide him timely notice that judgment had been entered. Rule 74.03 provides: Immediately upon the entry of an order or judgment, the clerk shall serve a notice of the entry by mail in the manner provided for in Rule 43.01 upon each party who is not in default for failure to appear and who was not present in court in person or by attorney at the time of the entry of such order or judgment.

In accordance with Rule 55.25(a), his answer was due “within thirty days after the service of the summons and petition,” which according to the record occurred on October 29, 2005, such that his answer was due on or before November 28, 2005.

During such hearing, the court shall ascertain whether: (1) The person sought to be adopted, if a child, has been in the lawful a…” / current text “1. interps.court: Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District
interps.citation: In the Interest of M.D.D., 219 S.W.3d 873 (Mo. App. S.D. 2007)
interps.summary: Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District opinion applying or construing § 211.447 RSMo (neutral index summary; see excerpts).
excerpts: For ease of discussion, we shall begin with the claim that the trial court failed to make specific findings as set forth in § 211.447.

We shall next address the merits of Point I. In reviewing whether the statutory grounds for termination under § 211.447.3-4 are supported by clear, cogent and convincing evidence, this Court will affirm the trial court’s decision unless the record contains no substantial evidence to support it, it is against the weight of the evidence, or the trial court erroneously declares or applies the law.

Jackson County Circuit Court, 162 S.W.3d 53, 61 (Mo.App.2005) (holding that in interpreting rules and statutes, courts are to give the language used its plain and ordinary meaning), it is clear that in providing that it is sufficient to allege “generally” that all conditions precedent have been performed or have occurred, the Missouri Supreme Court and the legislature did not intend, as the respondent contends, that the pleader can simply plead in total conclusory fashion, as the respondent did here in its petition, that “all conditions precedent have occurred, including but not limited to the giving of any Notice of Sale that may be required by law.”

The mandate of § 408.556.1, with respect to the pleading of facts to state a cause of action for a deficiency judgment, is consistent with the requirement of Rule 55.05, that a plaintiffs petition must “contain [] a short and plain statement of the facts showing that the pleader is entitled to relieff.]” The purpose of this fact-pleading requirement “is to present, define[,] and isolate the controverted issues so as to advise the trial court and the parties of the issues to be tried and to expedite the trial of a cause on the merits.”
Hence, to accept the respondent’s interpretation of Rule 55.16 and § 509.170, with respect to pleading compliance with § 400.9-610(b), would force us to ignore Rule 55.05.

excerpts: Section 452.410.1, which governs child custody modification, provides, in relevant part, that: the court shall not modify a prior custody decree unless ... it finds, upon the basis of facts that have arisen since the prior decree or that were unknown to the court at the time of the prior decree, that a change has occurred in the circumstances of the child or his custodian and that the modification is necessary to serve the best interests of the child.
While the issue was not raised by Mother, we note that the trial court’s judgment does not make any statutory findings as required by Section 452.375.6.

That section provides that: the court from time to time after considering all relevant factors including the financial resources of both parties, the merits of the case and the actions of the parties during the pendency of the action, may order a party to pay a reasonable amount for the cost to the other party of maintaining or defending any proceeding pursuant to sections 452.300 to 452.415 and for attorney’s fees, including sums for legal services rendered and costs incurred prior to the commencement of the proceeding and after entry of a final judgment.

The Supreme Court of Missouri held in Searcy, 8 S.W.3d at 117, that under the “plain language of [Section] 452.410.1, ... a moving party ... who seeks to modify a custody order must first establish that a substantial ‘change of circumstances of the child or his custodian’ has occurred.”

norms.b_justification: Functional review: the opinion (2007-03-15) applied § 452.410 RSMo as in force from 1990-08-28 (revisor bid 25044); current text in force since 2021-08-28. Interpreted subsection(s) identified from the opinion: 1. Compared subsection 1: version text “1. Except as provided in subsection 2 of this section, the court shall not modify a prior custody decree unless it has jurisdiction under the provisions of section 452.450 and it finds, upon the basis of facts that have …” / current text “1. Except as provided in subsection 2 of this section, the court shall not modify a prior custody decree unless it has jurisdiction under the provisions of section 452.745 and it finds, upon the basis of facts that have …”. The opinion interprets subsection 1's requirement that a change in the circumstances of the child or custodian occur and that modification serve the child's best interests. That interpreted language remains substantively unchanged; the current text only updates jurisdictional cross-references and modifies the separate joint-custody provision.

interps.summary: Missouri Court of Appeals opinion applying or construing Rule 81.13, Rule 81.12 (neutral index summary; see verbatim excerpts).
excerpts: Rule 81.13 provides a means for parties to set forth an agreed statement as to the record on appeal: When the questions presented by an appeal can be determined without an examination of all the pleadings, evidence and proceedings in the court below, the parties may prepare and sign a statement of the case showing how the questions arose and were decided in the trial court and setting forth only so many of the facts averred and proved or sought to be proved as are essential to a decision of the questions by the appellate court.

If a party petitions this Court for review of an issue, then it is his duty to provide “all of the record, proceedings and evidence necessary to the determination of all questions to be presented.” Rule 81.12(a); see also Davis v. Long, 521 S.W.2d 7, 8-9 (Mo.App.Spfld.D.1975).

If the statement conforms to the truth, it, together with such additions as the Court may consider necessary fully to present the questions raised by the appeal, shall be approved by the trial court and shall then be certified to the appellate court as the record on appeal. Rule 81.13.

norms.b_justification: Functional review: the opinion (2006-10-19) applied § 452.400 RSMo as in force from 2005-08-28 (revisor bid 51906); current text in force since 2016-08-28. (1) A parent not granted custody of the child is entitled to reasonable visitation rights unless the court finds, after a hearing, that visitation would endanger the child's physical health or impair his or her emotio…”; subsection 2: version text “2. (1) The court may modify an order granting or denying visitation rights whenever modification would serve the best interests of the child, but the court shall not restrict a parent's visitation rights unless it finds …” / current text “2. (1) The court may modify an order granting or denying visitation rights whenever modification would serve the best interests of the child, but the court shall not restrict a parent's visitation rights unless it finds …”. The opinion interprets subsection 1(4)'s requirement for specific findings concerning protection from further harm and subsection 2(1)'s requirement that visitation may be restricted only upon a finding of danger to the child's physical health or impairment of emotional development. When Mr. Elam’s motion was filed, Rule 24.035(b) required that such motions, where a direct appeal is not taken from the judgment or sentence, “shall be filed within ninety days of the date the person is delivered to the custody of the department of corrections.” . Rule 74.06(d), Missouri Rules of Civil Procedure, does not apply to judgments or orders entered in criminal matters.

In Scott v. State, 180 S.W.3d 519, 521 (Mo.App. W.D.2006), this court ruled that a docket entry overruling motions filed under Rules 24.035 and 74.06, which entry is accompanied by a judge’s typewritten initials, does not satisfy the signature requirement of Rule 74.01(a) of the Missouri Rules of Civil Procedure, and, thus, this court is without jurisdiction to hear an appeal of what would otherwise be an appealable order.
Mr. Elam then filed the pro se motion at issue here, seeking to withdraw his guilty plea, to vacate sentence, or for alternative relief from judgment under Rules 29.07(d) and 74.06(d).

interps.summary: Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District opinion applying or construing § 516.420 RSMo, § 516.130 RSMo, § 516.380 RSMo, § 516.120 RSMo, § 516.400 RSMo (neutral index summary; see verbatim excerpts).
excerpts: One of the affirmative defenses raised herein by defendants is the defense that the claims are barred by the statute of limitations set forth in section 516.130(2), RSMo 2000, which provides for a three-year period of limitations for actions on a statute for a penalty or forfeiture where the action is given to the party aggrieved. In response to defendants’ motions, plaintiffs asked for and were granted leave to file a third amended petition in which plaintiffs asserted that plaintiffs had six years in which to bring an action under section 516.420, which is applicable to claims for a penalty or forfeiture brought against “moneyed corporations” within the meaning of section 516.420.

Borrowers contend the proper statute of limitations is as follows: None of the provisions of sections 516.380 to 516.420 shall apply to suits against moneyed corporations or against the directors or stockholders thereof, to recover any penalty or forfeiture imposed, or to enforce any liability created by the act of incorporation or any other law; but all such suits shall be brought within six years after the discovery by the aggrieved party of the facts upon which such penalty or forfeiture attached, or by which such liability was created. § 516.420.

ULRICH and BRECKENRIDGE, JJ., concur. . All statutory references are to the Revised Statutes of Missouri 2000, unless otherwise indicated. . In making this argument, Respondents risk the possibility of the court believing that neither section. 516.130 nor 516.420 is applicable here, and therefore the applicable statute is section 516.120(2) which is a five-year statute.

excerpts: Because Mother’s motion to modify, seeking, inter alia, a modification of the trial court’s existing child support order, to require Father to pay her child support for Carrie, based on a change in Carrie’s physical custody from Father to Mother, which is governed by § 452.410, did not state a claim for such a modification, which is governed by § 452.370, the court was deprived of subject matter jurisdiction and had no authority to enter the child support order Father challenges on appeal.

Section 452.340.2 provides, in pertinent part: The obligation of the parent ordered to make support payments shall abate, in whole or in part, for such periods of time in excess of thirty consecutive days that the other parent has voluntarily relinquished physical custody of a child to the parent ordered to pay support, notwithstanding any periods of visitation or temporary physical and legal or physical or legal custody pursuant to a judgment of dissolution or legal separation or any modification thereof.

Rule 55.05, which, pursuant to Rule 41.01(a)(2), is applicable to a modifieation-of-child-support proceeding in the circuit court, requires, in pertinent part, that a “pleading that sets forth a claim for relief ... contain [ ] a short and plain statement of the facts showing the pleader is entitled to relief.”

Timmerman, 139 S.W.3d 230, 234 (Mo.App.2004), “custody,” as defined in § 452.375.1(3), does not include “primary physical custody” as a statutorily permissible physical custodial arrangement, only joint or sole physical custody.

norms.b_justification: Functional review: the opinion (2006-05-02) applied § 452.410 RSMo as in force from 1990-08-28 (revisor bid 25044); current text in force since 2021-08-28. Interpreted subsection(s) identified from the opinion: 1. Compared subsection 1: version text “1. Except as provided in subsection 2 of this section, the court shall not modify a prior custody decree unless it has jurisdiction under the provisions of section 452.450 and it finds, upon the basis of facts that have …” / current text “1. Except as provided in subsection 2 of this section, the court shall not modify a prior custody decree unless it has jurisdiction under the provisions of section 452.745 and it finds, upon the basis of facts that have …”. The opinion interprets subsection 1’s requirement that a custody modification be based on changed or previously unknown facts, a change in circumstances, and the child’s best interests. That rule is unchanged; the jurisdictional cross-reference was updated from § 452.450 to § 452.745, while the separately stated joint-custody provision was not part of the opinion’s interpretation.

The opinion (2006-05-02) predates the current version of § 452.370 RSMo (in force since 2014-08-28) but quotes the statutory/rule language it interprets — “may be modified only upon a showing of changed circumstances so substantial and continuing as to make the terms unreasonable.” — and that language appears verbatim in the current text; the interpreted language is therefore identical in wording and function.

The obligation of the parent ordered to make support payments shall abate, in whole or in part, for such periods of time in excess of thirty consecutive days that the other parent has voluntarily relinquished physical…” / current text “2. The obligation of the parent ordered to make support payments shall abate, in whole or in part, for such periods of time in excess of thirty consecutive days that the other parent has voluntarily relinquished physical…”. The opinion interprets § 452.340.2, particularly the rule that support abates when the other parent voluntarily relinquishes physical custody for more than thirty consecutive days and that no court-ordered custody change is required. That interpreted language is unchanged in the current subsection; only administrative provisions elsewhere in subsection 2 use updated terminology and wording.

interps.summary: Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District opinion applying or construing § 452.330, § 452.300, § 452.415 RSMo (neutral index summary; see excerpts).
excerpts: Husband claims the trial court did not properly apply section 452.330, RSMo 2000, and should have awarded him all but $300 of the insurance proceeds because the value of Wife’s marital property destroyed by the fire was less than $300.

Section 452.330.2 states: For purposes of sections 452.300 to 452.415 only, "marital property” means all property acquired by either spouse subsequent to the marriage except: (1) Property acquired by gift, bequest, devise, or descent; (2) Property acquired in exchange for property acquired prior to the marriage or in exchange for property acquired by gift, bequest, devise, or descent; (3) Property acquired by a spouse after a decree of legal separation; (4) Property excluded by valid written agreement of the parties; and (5) The increase in value of property acquired prior to the marriage or pursuant to subdivisions (1) to (4) of this subsection, unless marital assets including labor, have contributed to such increases and then only to the extent of such contributions.

Section 452.330.3 provides that “[a]ll property acquired by either spouse subsequent to the marriage and prior to a decree of legal separation or dissolution of marriage is presumed to be marital property ... [, unless t]he presumption of marital property is overcome by a showing that the property was acquired by a method listed in subsection 2 of this section.”
Without a “valid written agreement” of the parties to make the items of personal property nonmarital, as required by section 452.330.2(4), it retained its character as marital property.

Rule 54.20(b)(1) provides: Every officer to whom summons or other process shall be delivered for service outside the state shall make an affidavit before the clerk or judge of the court of which affiant is an officer or other person authorized to administer oaths in such state stating the time, place and manner of such service, the official character of the affiant, and the affiant’s authority to serve process in civil actions within the state or territory where such service was made.

excerpts: Section 516.100 describes “accrued” as: “the cause of action shall not be deemed to accrue when the wrong is done or the technical breach of contract or duty occurs, but when the damage resulting therefrom is sustained and is capable of ascertainment^]” So, for the purpose of applying § 516.190, a “cause of action shall not be deemed to” originate where “the wrong is done or the technical breach of contract or duty occurs, but,” where “the damage resulting therefrom is sustained and capable of ascertainment.”

For the purpose of determining where a cause of action “originates,” courts look to when a cause of action “accrues,” as set forth in § 516.100 and have equated “originated” with “accrued,” as used in that statute.

As the court went on to explain: Section 516.300 is designed to assure the Missouri general statute of limitations will not be injected into a cause of action that has its own built-in statute of limitations.

excerpts: The recognized purpose for Rule 84.04(c) — the “statement of facts” rule — is to afford an immediate, accurate, complete, and unbiased understanding of the facts of the case.

We note that Rule 84.04 provides the standards that all must follow when proceeding with an appeal. Under that rule, a brief must contain, inter alia: (1) a concise jurisdictional statement; (2) a statement of facts; (3) points relied on; (4) an argument which substantially follows the order of the points relied on; and (5) a short conclusion stating the precise relief sought.

Legal Analysis: A. STATUTORY FINDINGS The trial court terminated Mother’s and Father’s parental rights under section 211.447.4(3), which allows the filing and granting of a termination petition when it is in the best interests of the child, the child has been under the jurisdiction of the juvenile court for one year, when the conditions leading to assumption of jurisdiction or other potentially harmful conditions persist, when little likelihood exists that those conditions can be remedied at an early date or when continuing the parental relationship greatly diminishes any prospect for the child’s early integration into a stable and permanent home.

Id. II. Discussion In their brief, defendants assert, in separately lettered subpoints, that plaintiff failed to satisfy the mandatory prerequisites of Rule 52.08(a) because the named plaintiff is not an adequate class representative as required by Rule 52.08(a)(4) (Sub-point G).

norms.b_justification: The opinion (2005-08-16) predates the current version of Rule 52.08 (in force since 2026-01-01) but quotes the language it applies — “predominate over any questions affecting only individual members” — and that language appears verbatim (normalized for punctuation/case) in the current text; the interpreted language is therefore identical in wording and function.

excerpts: Under the directions for use of Form No. 14, parties required to complete said form are “[t]he parent obligated to pay support and the parent entitled to receive support[J” See also Rule 88.01.

Section 454.400, RSMo 2000 establishes the Division of Child Support Enforcement “to administer the state plan for child support enforcement,]” including the ability “to adopt, amend and repeal rules and regulations.”
Supreme Court Rule 88.01(a) grants administrative agencies the right to determine child support payments using “all relevant factors, including statutorily relevant factors.”
Rule 88.01(b) makes the amount calculated a rebuttable presumption.

norms.b_justification: The opinion (2005-08-12) predates the current version of § 454.400 RSMo (in force since 2014-08-28) but quotes the statutory/rule language it interprets — “to administer the state plan for child support enforcement,]” — and that language appears verbatim in the current text; the interpreted language is therefore identical in wording and function.

interps.court: Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District
interps.citation: Y.O. v. Barton County Juvenile Office, 169 S.W.3d 152 (Mo. App. S.D. 2005)
interps.summary: Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District opinion applying or construing § 211.455, § 211.477 RSMo (neutral index summary; see excerpts).
excerpts: Section 211.455 also states that “[t]he court shall order an investigation and social study” in cases involving the involuntary termination of parental rights and directs that “[t]he investigation and social study shall be made by the juvenile officer, the state division of family services or a public or private agency authorized or licensed to care for children or any other competent person, as directed by the courtf.]” In this case, the written report of the “investigation and social study,” was prepared by the Children’s Division and filed simultaneously with the petition for termination on November 20, 2003.

Within thirty days after the juvenile officer and the court have met pursuant to section 211.455,the court shall hold the disposi-tional hearing_” Section 211.477.1, RSMo 2000, now provides, in pertinent part: If, after the dispositional hearing, the court finds that one or more of the grounds set out in section 211.447 exists ... and that it is in the best interests of the child, the court may terminate the rights of parent in and to the child.

The written report of the investigation and social study contemplated by section 211.455 is mandatory, In the Interest of T.G., 965 S.W.2d 326, 332 (Mo.App. 1998), and is intended to aid the court “in determining whether termination of parental rights is in the child’s best interest.”

norms.b_justification: Functional review: the opinion (2005-08-11) applied § 211.455 RSMo as in force from 1985-09-28 (revisor bid 58713); current text in force since 2014-08-28. Interpreted subsection(s) identified from the opinion: 3. Compared subsection 3: version text “3. The court shall order an investigation and social study except in cases filed under section 211.444. The investigation and social study shall be made by the juvenile officer, the state division of family services or a…” / current text “3. The court shall order an investigation and social study except in cases filed under section 211.444. The investigation and social study shall be made by the juvenile officer, the state children's division or a public …”. The opinion interprets subsection 3, particularly its requirement that the court order a written investigation and social study to aid in determining the child’s best interests. That requirement and its function are unchanged; only the agency designation changed from the “state division of family services” to the “state children’s division.”

Functional review: the opinion (2005-08-11) applied § 211.477 RSMo as in force from 2003-08-28 (revisor bid 52680); current text in force since 2014-08-28. Interpreted subsection(s) identified from the opinion: 1. Compared subsection 1: version text “1. If, after the dispositional hearing, the court finds that one or more of the grounds set out in section 211.447 exists or that the parent has consented to the termination pursuant to section 211.444 and that it is in …” / current text “1. If, after the dispositional hearing, the court finds that one or more of the grounds set out in section 211.447 exists or that the parent has consented to the termination pursuant to section 211.444 and that it is in …”. The opinion interprets subsection 1, particularly the court’s authority to terminate parental rights after finding statutory grounds and that termination is in the child’s best interests. That termination rule is unchanged; only the post-termination custody designation changed from the “division of family services” to the “children’s division.”

interps.court: Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District
interps.citation: Johnson v. Missouri Department of Health & Senior Services, 174 S.W.3d 568 (Mo. App. W.D. 2005)
interps.summary: Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District opinion applying or construing Rule 84.04 (neutral index summary; see verbatim excerpts).
excerpts: Compliance with Rule 84.04 briefing requirements is mandatory in order to ensure that appellate courts do not become advocates by speculating on facts and on arguments that have not been made.

Rule 84.04(d)(1) provides: (1) Where the appellate court reviews the decision of a trial court, each point shall: (A) identify the trial court ruling or action that the appellant challenges; (B) state concisely the legal reasons for the appellant’s claim of reversible error; and (C) explain in summary fashion why, in the context of the case, those legal reasons support the claim of reversible error.
Her point is nothing more than an abstract statement of the law, which is unacceptable in satisfying the requirements of Rule 84.04(d).

norms.b_justification: The opinion (2005-08-09) predates the current version of Rule 84.04 (in force since 2018-01-01) but quotes the language it applies — “The trial court erred in [identify the challenged ruling or action], because [state the legal reasons for the claim of reversible error], in that [explain why the legal reasons, in the context of the case, support the claim of reversible error].” — and that language appears verbatim (normalized for punctuation/case) in the current text; the interpreted language is therefore identical in wording and function.
